added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: there is definitely a little bit of a debate among um CTA practitioners um for sure and I don't know that that many of our colleagues have embraced them.
added_claims.claim: Adoption of single-stock futures among CTAs is mixed: a minority strongly favour trading single names rather than only indices, while most CTAs still stick to index futures.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: if you were long only NASDAQ in 2001ish um you would have been down 85% at some point
added_claims.claim: Long-only equity exposure is not low blow-up risk: a long-only Nasdaq position fell about 85% in the 2000-2002 bust, so a low blow-up ranking for long-only equity is questionable.

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: As you go to further out on the curve, suddenly you're moving to the new crop. You really don't know what is going to be the supply.
added_claims.claim: In agricultural curves the front is driven by demand because the crop size is already largely known, while deferred contracts (new crop) are driven by supply risks such as weather and disease, so different maturities carry distinct risk factors and different diversification value.
added_claims.conditions: applies to crops with a harvest cycle (cotton, wheat)
added_claims.testable: yes - return correlation between front and deferred contracts

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: natural gas is an example um you know for example we would calculate the volatility on a specific contract or we would make the adjustment to when you roll the position in order to manage the risk slightly better
added_claims.claim: Where adjacent contracts differ materially in volatility (natural gas summer versus winter), a trend manager can compute volatility for the specific contract or adjust position size at the roll, so risk stays constant across the roll; for most markets using the rolled front series is still valid and there is no single correct answer.
added_claims.conditions: natural gas and other seasonal contracts
added_claims.testable: yes - compare realised portfolio volatility with and without roll adjustment

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: I think that mechanism that causes it is more the options.
added_claims.claim: Launching single-stock futures should not reduce single-stock dispersion because the cause is the index options explosion (0DTE), not the ease of shorting; single-stock options are less liquid and the CME contracts cover only about 50 very liquid names.
added_claims.testable: partly - monitor dispersion after the single-stock futures launch

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: we've seen a little bit in like in bond futures we've seen that um so we've seen again moving to weekly options at different days expiry um a little bit in oil and stuff like that.
added_claims.claim: Short-dated and weekly option expiries are spreading from equity indices to bond futures and oil, so the options-gamma mechanism that suppresses equity index trends could appear in other markets, with implications for short-term trend following there.
added_claims.indicator: weekly option volumes in bond futures and oil
added_claims.conditions: if option volume in those markets concentrates at-the-money near expiry
added_claims.testable: yes - test autocorrelation changes as short-dated option volume grows

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: they look at within each asset class what is the variation. uh the picture there is actually a lot more nuanced I would say
added_claims.claim: The CFM tick-size result is driven mainly by cross-asset differences (equities now have a much smaller volatility-adjusted tick than bonds); within each asset class the relationship is more nuanced, so the equity index finding should not be generalised to every market.
added_claims.indicator: volatility-adjusted tick size by asset class

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: we have seen maybe a drop of 3% in autocorrelation in the equity market over over the last 20 years.
added_claims.claim: One-day autocorrelation in equity returns has fallen by about three percentage points over roughly 20 years, enough to cost fast equity trend followers about 0.2 Sharpe while leaving slower, macro-driven trend followers largely unaffected.
added_claims.testable: yes - rolling autocorrelation of index returns

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: in the absence of complete information in the market, the fact that the price has gone up or the fact that other people are talking about a theme actually makes you evaluate your own valuation
added_claims.claim: Narrative underreaction has a rational explanation: with incomplete information, investors infer value from price moves and from what others discuss, so slow-moving themes diffuse gradually; fast, obvious themes such as war are priced instantly and show no lag.
added_claims.conditions: slow-evolving themes only; instant for obvious shocks such as war
added_claims.testable: yes - test underreaction by theme speed

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: I actually like the way that they do an uh a human overlay of the basket for the themes that they're doing.
added_claims.claim: Because statistical stock-to-narrative betas are noisy, one bank's QIS theme baskets add a human overlay (for example judging that Coca-Cola benefits from the World Cup even if it is not visible in price), which is sensible economically but non-quantitative and hard for a systematic manager to trade.
added_claims.testable: partly - human-curated basket construction cannot be replicated systematically

added_claims.speaker: Yoav Git
added_claims.quote: you're not just catching up to trend you're also catching up to the risk factor which is trading right now.
added_claims.claim: Narrative-based equity trend is harder than the other layers because the narrative covers only about 5% of variance and its identity keeps changing, so a manager has to track both the trend and which risk factor is currently live.
added_claims.testable: partly - requires a point-in-time news dataset

corrections.issue: Unit inconsistency: Git's 'basis points of Sharpe' mean hundredths of a Sharpe ratio (16bp = 0.16, 3bp = 0.03, 6bp = 0.06, about 20bp = 0.2). The first-reader text mixes '0.16 Sharpe' with '3bp' and '6bp', which reads as 0.0003 and 0.0006 Sharpe.
corrections.fix: A 1% fall in one-day autocorrelation costs a trader using yesterday's price about 0.16 Sharpe (1% times about 16, the square root of roughly 256 trading days), but a 5/20-day crossover with roughly one-fifth weight on the one-day effect loses only about 0.03 Sharpe per market, or about 0.06 across a lightly diversified equity portfolio; a 3% fall therefore costs about 0.2 Sharpe for short-term traders and much less for slower (two-month) trend followers.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured the CFM market-structure chain (0DTE gamma, dispersion, tick size), the commodity-contract answer and narrative momentum accurately; it missed secondary mechanisms and examples (maturity-specific ag risk, roll volatility adjustment, rational basis of underreaction, QIS human overlay, spread of short-dated options) and one unit mix-up.
